Marketplace is a modern web-based surplus food management and redistribution system developed using the MERN stack and integrated with real-time communication and automated food management technologies. Designed to reduce food wastage, improve accessibility to affordable food, and promote environmental sustainability, the system connects three primary user roles: Customer, Restaurant Partner, and System Administrator, each providing features tailored to its specific responsibilities within the platform.

The system enables customers to discover surplus food items from verified restaurants, bakeries, and cafes at discounted prices ranging from 50% to 80% off the original price. Customers can search and filter food listings based on name, cuisine, price, dietary preferences, allergens, and Surprise Bag availability. The platform supports online reservation through a simulated payment process, generates digital receipts in PDF format, and provides a unique six-digit collection OTP along with a QR code for secure order pickup. Customers can also cancel reservations subject to the applicable order status, with the system restoring the reserved quantity to the available inventory. Ratings and reviews can be submitted after order collection, helping maintain restaurant ratings and improve customer confidence.

To improve operational efficiency, the system integrates Socket.io for real-time order notifications and provides a dual-verification mechanism through manual OTP entry and camera-based QR code scanning. The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is a standardized modeling language used to specify, visualize, construct, and document the components and architecture of software systems. It provides a set of graphical notations and diagrams that help developers represent the design of complex systems in a clear and structured manner. UML is widely adopted in software engineering due to its ability to standardize the design process, improve communication among team members, and support systematic development practices. UML plays a crucial role in object-oriented software development, allowing designers to represent the relationships between classes, objects, and user interactions effectively. By using UML diagrams such as use case diagrams, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, and activity diagrams, project teams can explore different design alternatives, validate the architecture, and ensure that all functional and non-functional requirements

UML also aids in identifying system constraints and dependencies early in the development process. By visualizing the interactions between different modules and components, developers can detect potential bottlenecks, redundant processes, or conflicting functionalities before implementation. This reduces errors during coding, minimizes development time, and improves overall system efficiency. For example, in

, UML diagrams help illustrate how the user module interacts with the admin module, the database, and external services like Google authentication and payment gateways, ensuring smooth integration and operation of all components.
